name: Australian meat pie
summary: A hand-sized pastry case filled with minced or diced beef in gravy, usually eaten with tomato sauce.
story: The Australian meat pie descends from British pie-making, brought by colonists and adapted with local beef. It became everyday takeaway food sold at bakeries, service stations, and sports grounds, where eating a pie with tomato sauce is a familiar ritual. Pies come with many fillings now, but the plain beef pie remains the standard.

origin_claims.claim: Derived from British savoury pies brought to the colonies in the 19th century.
Eating a pie with tomato sauce at the football is a defining Australian habit.

name: Lamington
summary: Squares of light sponge dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in desiccated coconut.
story: The lamington is named after a governor of Queensland, Lord Lamington, who held the post at the end of the 19th century, though how the cake came to carry his name is told in several ways. Printed recipes appear in early 20th-century Queensland. It is a staple of school fundraisers, bake sales, and Australia Day tables.

origin_claims.claim: Named after Lord Lamington, governor of Queensland from 1896 to 1901.
A cook accidentally dropped sponge into chocolate and the result pleased the governor.
New Zealand also claims the cake.

name: Anzac biscuits
summary: Chewy oat and coconut biscuits sweetened with golden syrup, tied to Anzac Day remembrance.
story: These biscuits are linked to the First World War and to the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (Anzac). They are often said to have been baked by women at home and sent to soldiers, though how many were actually posted is debated, and early recipes were also sold to raise funds. In Australia the name 'Anzac' is protected and biscuits sold under it are expected to follow a traditional recipe. New Zealand has its own version and a long-running friendly argument over who baked them first.

origin_claims.claim: Baked at home and sent to troops overseas during the First World War.
Early recipes appeared in wartime fundraising and cookbooks.
Origin is claimed in both Australia and New Zealand.

name: Damper
summary: A simple soda bread baked in campfire ashes or an oven, traditionally eaten with golden syrup or butter.
story: Damper is the bush bread of drovers and stockmen, made with flour, water and salt and baked in the coals so it needs no oven or yeast. It is closely tied to outback travel and camping. Long before wheat arrived, Aboriginal people made seed cakes from ground native grass seeds and other plants, which is a separate and much older tradition that damper later sat alongside.

origin_claims.claim: Developed by colonial-era stockmen and drovers who needed bread without an oven.
Aboriginal seed-cake traditions predate wheat flour in Australia.

name: Sausage sizzle
summary: Barbecued sausages served in a slice of white bread with fried onion and sauce.
story: The sausage sizzle is a community fundraising ritual: a barbecue set up outside a hardware store, school or polling place, serving a sausage folded in a slice of bread. At elections it is nicknamed the 'democracy sausage'. It is also a common part of a summer barbecue on Australia Day.

origin_claims.claim: A fundraising barbecue tradition at schools, clubs, and election polling places.

name: Barramundi with lemon myrtle
summary: Pan-seared barramundi fillets finished with butter and lemon myrtle, a native rainforest leaf.
story: Barramundi is a large fish of northern Australian rivers, estuaries and coasts, long fished by Aboriginal peoples and now farmed as well. Its name is thought to come from an Aboriginal language of Queensland. Lemon myrtle is a rainforest tree whose leaves taste strongly of lemon and have become a popular native flavouring in modern Australian cooking. Pairing them is a contemporary dish rather than an old one.

origin_claims.claim: Barramundi has long been a food fish for northern Aboriginal communities.
Lemon myrtle came into wide culinary use in Australian restaurants from the late 20th century.

name: Pan-seared kangaroo fillet
summary: A very lean kangaroo fillet seared quickly and served with a red wine pan sauce.
story: Kangaroo has been eaten by Aboriginal peoples for many thousands of years. Selling it for human consumption became widespread in Australia only in the late 20th century, and it now appears in supermarkets and restaurants. The meat is dark and very lean, so it is best cooked fast and left rare to medium-rare.

origin_claims.claim: A long-standing food of Aboriginal peoples.
Became widely sold for general consumption in the late 20th century.

name: Vegemite on toast
summary: Hot buttered toast with a thin scrape of Vegemite, a dark salty yeast-extract spread.
story: Vegemite is a spread made from brewers' yeast extract, developed in Melbourne in the early 1920s for the Fred Walker company in response to a shortage of imported British yeast spreads. It is salty and intensely savoury, so it is spread very thinly. Buttered toast with Vegemite is a common breakfast and lunchbox food, and the yeast extract is itself a preserved, fermented-derived product.

origin_claims.claim: Developed in Melbourne in the early 1920s as a local alternative to imported yeast extracts.

name: Sydney rock oysters
summary: Freshly opened rock oysters served natural with lemon or a sharp vinegar dressing.
story: The Sydney rock oyster is native to the south-eastern coast, and shell middens left by Aboriginal people along the coast show that oysters have been eaten there for a very long time. Oyster farming grew in the 19th and 20th centuries on estuaries in New South Wales. They are most often eaten raw and plain, straight from the shell.

origin_claims.claim: Eaten along the coast by Aboriginal people for thousands of years.
Commercial oyster farming developed on New South Wales estuaries from the 19th century.

name: Pie floater
summary: A meat pie served upside down in a bowl of thick green pea soup and topped with tomato sauce.
story: The pie floater is a speciality of Adelaide, South Australia, traditionally sold from pie carts late at night. A baked meat pie is set in a bowl of green pea soup and finished with tomato sauce. It is closely tied to the city's pie-cart history and is now found in some pubs and cafes as a local novelty.

origin_claims.claim: Associated with Adelaide pie carts, which sold hot food to late-night crowds.
